indicators.note: spurious means false or not genuine, so the letters of these three words are faked into a new order

explanation.surface: Sugar was fed to someone as a phoney assurance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spurious' rearranges SUGARFEDA, all nine letters of the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A safeguard is a protective measure, something that guarantees security.

indicators.note: the word riot could be produced from these letters, so the clue says they cause it once rearranged

explanation.surface: A competitor on a reality show might start a riot.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition '8' means the answer to 8 down, a television show about learners, so it stands for a beginner; 'could cause' says that the letters rearranged produce RIOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiro is a novice or beginner, someone still learning, like a contestant on a show for learners.

clue.text: Banned at St Tropez one's large pants

parts.note: in French, as spoken in St Tropez, one is un
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
pants is British slang for rubbish, very bad

explanation.surface: Something forbidden on a French Riviera beach: a man's oversized underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like underwear but is British slang for poor quality, so it means AWFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something banned is prohibited by law, illegal.

clue.text: When river rises in Italian town

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he arrived'

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the word is read upwards, so it is turned round

parts.note: the Isis is the name of the Thames at Oxford

explanation.surface: Asking when a river floods in an Italian town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rises' fits a down clue, where the river's name is read from the bottom upwards; the Isis is the Thames as it flows through Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria, birthplace of St Francis.

clue.text: Attack like mad dog — that's heartless

indicators.note: heartless means the central letter of the word for a mad dog is taken away

parts.note: a mad dog is one with rabies, rabid

explanation.surface: An assault as savage as a crazed dog's, without compassion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' removes B, the middle letter of RABID.
explanation.definitionFit: A raid is a sudden assault or attack on a place.

parts.note: a tab is a bill, as in picking up the tab
by can mean near or close to, as in 'stand by me'

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill gets near a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is the bill you pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabby is a striped domestic cat.

parts.note: an and a are the same indefinite article
a lie is a falsehood, here jokingly called an exaggeration
nates is the Latin anatomical word for the buttocks

explanation.surface: An overstatement at its root puts people's backs up.
explanation.walkthrough: NATES, Latin for buttocks, is a crossword favourite for 'bottom'.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate someone is to make them hostile or estranged, to antagonise them.

clue.text: Show one's definitely got something to learn

definitions.text: one's definitely got something to learn

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the BBC reality series fronted by Alan Sugar; the second is a learner indentured to a skilled worker.
explanation.definitionFit: A television show where business hopefuls compete, and a learner bound to an employer to master a trade.

indicators.note: backed means the word for the pub is written backwards

parts.note: boozer is British slang for a pub, a bar

explanation.surface: Someone put money on a horse in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' looks like betting on the horse, but it is the reversal signal; 'boozer' is British slang for a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arab is a breed of horse famous for speed and stamina.

indicators.note: move tells the solver to shift the letters of these two words around

explanation.surface: A sad story that stirs the emotions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' looks like being moved to tears, but it rearranges TALEDOES.
explanation.definitionFit: Desolate means wretched and forlorn, utterly unhappy.

indicators.note: arranged means the letters of the following words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of organising a group of musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' looks musical, but it is the anagram signal for 'a band'; I stands as it is in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An indaba is a conference or council, a word from southern Africa.

indicators.note: reactionary suggests moving backwards, so the word for shock is written in reverse

parts.note: to shock someone is to stun them

explanation.surface: An ardent fan likes to shock conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reactionary' looks political, but it reverses STUN.
explanation.definitionFit: To be nuts about something is to be enthusiastic, passionate about it.

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded in family trees
a mart is a market

explanation.surface: A sharp trader did well at the market.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart means intelligent, quick-witted.

clue.text: Field of ponies? To start with that's silly and affected

indicators.note: to start with means the opening letter of each of the preceding words is taken

parts.note: pish is an exclamation dismissing something as nonsense

explanation.surface: A meadow full of ponies, a silly and pretentious idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To start with' takes F, O, P from 'Field of ponies'; PISH is an old exclamation of contempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Foppish describes a dandy, vain and pretentious, overly concerned with fine dress.

indicators.note: going means the letter given in the bracket departs from the word for films

parts.note: to film a scene is to shoot it
the letter S, printed as a bare initial

explanation.surface: Filming something with a dash missing makes people laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' removes S from SHOOTS; the bracket's S with dashes names the letter to drop.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoots are loud bursts of laughter.

indicators.note: carrying means the words hold the answer inside them

explanation.surface: Someone appeared bearing a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' shows the answer is held across 'Came up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Meu, also called spignel or baldmoney, is a mountain herb of the carrot family.

clue.text: Hear robes disguised American's skin condition

indicators.note: disguised means the letters of these words are put into a different form

explanation.surface: Listen: the gowns hide an American's skin problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disguised' rearranges HEARROBES; the answer uses the US spelling, without the O of British seborrhoea.
explanation.definitionFit: Seborrhea is a disorder of the oil glands causing scaly, greasy skin.

parts.note: are is a form of the verb to be, meaning exist or live

indicators.note: close to here means the final letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Living near Granada in a Spanish district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' looks like nearness but takes the last letter of Granada, A.
explanation.definitionFit: An area is a region or district.

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the word leader
not tells the solver the letter for united is absent from the word for row

parts.note: to row, rhyming with cow, is to argue
U is the abbreviation for united, as in football club names

explanation.surface: The Liberal leader's first quarrel shows a divided party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' looks like the party but is the definition, generous; L, the first letter of 'leader's', starts it.
explanation.definitionFit: Large can mean generous or broad-minded, as in a large heart.

clue.text: Toothless creatures in garden and vale

parts.note: Eden is the biblical garden
vale is Latin for farewell, and ta-ta is an informal goodbye

explanation.surface: Animals without teeth live in a garden and a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vale' looks like a valley but is the Latin farewell, two syllables, so TATA.
explanation.definitionFit: Edentata is the old name for an order of mammals, such as sloths and anteaters, lacking front teeth.

parts.note: O is the zero digit, nothing
in cricket the on side is also called the leg side

explanation.surface: A Russian says nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the on side and leg side are the same half of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: Oleg is a common Russian man's name.

parts.note: to do something is to perform it

explanation.surface: A young woman arrives in time to perform.
explanation.definitionFit: Dot is a girl's name, short for Dorothy.

clue.text: 8 put right back to start of course

clue.text: Old commentator and Cockney pro in conversation

indicators.note: in conversation means the word is spoken rather than written

parts.note: a pro is a prostitute, and an East Londoner's own word for one is 'arlot

explanation.surface: A former broadcaster and an East Ender's professional are chatting.
explanation.walkthrough: John Arlott was a much-loved BBC cricket commentator; Cockney speakers drop initial H, so harlot sounds like his name.
explanation.definitionFit: John Arlott was a radio cricket commentator, famous from the 1940s to 1980.

clue.text: Hard work ends without a return

indicators.note: return means the remaining letters are read backwards
without means the letter A is removed from the word for ends

parts.note: the ends of a football pitch are the goals

explanation.surface: Laborious toil is over, with nothing to show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' takes A out of GOALS to give GOLS, then 'return' reverses that.
explanation.definitionFit: A slog is a long tiring spell of effort.

indicators.note: fanciful means imaginative, so the letters of quote are rearranged freely

explanation.surface: An imaginative quotation is stale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old hat' looks like a phrase for something stale, but it means a hat of old style.
explanation.definitionFit: A toque is a small brimless hat, worn in the 16th century and by chefs today.

clue.text: German engineer without a current memorial

indicators.note: to engineer something is to construct it, so the remaining letters are built into a new order
without means letters are taken out of memorial

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current
taken as written

explanation.surface: A German engineer builds a monument without electricity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes I and A from MEMORIAL, leaving MEMORL, which 'engineer' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Erwin Rommel was a German field marshal, the Desert Fox of the Second World War.

clue.text: Extreme masculinity — that's not half an illusion

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
not half means only the first half of the word that is kept

explanation.surface: Macho maleness isn't half the deception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extreme' takes M and Y from masculinity; 'not half' keeps TH, half of 'that'.
explanation.definitionFit: A myth is a widely held but false belief, a fiction.

indicators.note: squash means crush, so the letters of these words are squeezed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Sports fans singing about squash or tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squash' looks like the racket sport but rearranges ORTENNIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Intoners are people who recite in a singing tone.

parts.note: no means none, a lack of
to OK something is to approve or support it

explanation.surface: Without backing, someone looks for a hideaway.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a secluded corner, a place of retreat.

indicators.note: keeps means the word for yet holds the next piece inside

parts.note: but means yet, however

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of smiling

explanation.surface: Penniless, yet keeping cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' puts S, the first letter of smiling, inside BUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Bust means bankrupt, out of money.

clue.text: Not yet working round city? It's our hero's age

indicators.note: round means the rearranged letters go around the word for city
working means the letters are put into action in a new arrangement

parts.note: a wen is a large city; London was called the Great Wen

explanation.surface: Someone not yet employed around town reaches adulthood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges 'Not yet' to TTYONE, and 'round' wraps it around the city; the hero is the 8-down learner, and 21 was the traditional coming of age.
explanation.definitionFit: Twenty-one was the traditional coming of age, when a young person came of age.
